lessons.title: split from d-orbital shape to crystal field
lessons.summary: Using the same set of real spherical harmonic coordinates, understand how the five orbitals are grouped by point group and what exactly the splitting parameters represent.

sections.title: five orbitals and ten single electron states
sections.text: Choose five normalized real d spherical harmonics xy, yz, xz, x²−y² and 3z²−r², each with ↑ and ↓. The ten-dimensional matrix describes ten single-electron basis states, not ten electrons automatically present in the system. Orbital colors show signs of real basis functions; radius illustrates angular distributions without an actual atomic radial scale.
sections.formula: d orbital space dimension 2l+1=5; single electron dimension of d⊗spin 5×2=10

sections.title: Two sets of energy of the octahedron maintain the center of gravity
sections.text: In ideal Oh coordination, xy,yz,xz form t₂g and the other two orbitals form e_g. Define Δ=E(e_g)−E(t₂g)>0 and place the five-orbital energy barycenter at zero to fix both sets of energies. Changing Δ changes energies only, not ligand bond lengths automatically.

sections.title: Tetrahedra order and label
sections.text: ideal Td context, the double e is lower than the triple t₂. Td has no inversion and no g/u is added to the label. The Δ entered here is the positive splitting amount of the current geometry; the same value is not treated as a coordination conversion of the same real material, nor is the empirical ratio between octahedron and tetrahedron automatically applied.

sections.title: The difference between material background and model
sections.text: NiO is the material background for learning the localized octahedron crystal field , but the d⁸ problem of Ni²⁺ also requires information on interactions between electrons, Hund multiplet and other information. This experiment does not have these terms, so it only shows the single-electron symmetry and the given energy level parameters. The high and low spin or ground state of the real material cannot be announced by the energy level diagram alone.
sections.formula: single-electron crystal field spectrum ≠ multi-electron multiplet spectrum ≠ material magnetic ground state prediction

lessons.title: tetragonal crystal field , SOC and degenerate subspaces
lessons.summary: goes from explicit Ds/Dt level parameters into full L·S coupling, distinguishing repeatable subspace information from arbitrary eigenbases.

sections.title: Ds and Dt are energy level parameters
sections.text: Here tetragonal terms act on the five d orbitals with specified diagonal coefficients, and Δ=10Dq for Oh. Ds/Dt are not fitted from ligand coordinates; their signs cannot be called elongation or compression independently of the convention. The 3D ligands still show an ideal background. Connecting distortions requires a separate mapping from displacements to crystal-field parameters.

sections.title: SOC mixes states throughout the full ten-dimensional space
sections.text: Angular-momentum matrices are transformed from l=2 raising/lowering operators into the real-orbital basis used by the 3D plot. L and S use units of ℏ, and λ uses eV. At zero crystal field, j=l±s gives an independently checkable analytical limit. Negative λ reverses the two level-group orderings without changing matrix or angular-momentum conventions.
sections.formula: H=H_CF⊗I₂+λL·S; E_j=λ[j(j+1)−l(l+1)−s(s+1)]/2; j=3/2:−3λ/2（4 state), j=5/2:λ（6 state)

sections.title: Kramers Pairing and stable angular density
sections.text: This model has no external magnetic field or other time reversal breaking terms, and the spin 1/2 enable level is at least Kramers pairs. A single eigenvector in a degenerate subspace can be arbitrary change of basis , so the main graph shows the angular density averaged over that subspace, traced over the spins. It is invariant under change of basis inside the subspace; the sum of the orbital projection weights is 1, not the multi-electron occupation number.

lessons.title: E⊗e: Distorted potential energy surface obtained from electron splitting
lessons.summary: Use an independent doublet model to derive two adiabatic potential energy surfaces, minimum radius and stabilization energy, and understand the extent of the circular valley.

sections.title: First indicate the two electronic states and two coordinates
sections.text: This section independently takes the two-fold electron basis [z²,x²−y²] and the two dimensionless reduced coordinates Q₂ and Q₃. The linear coupling is specified by a real coefficient g, and the elastic coefficient K must be positive. The ten-dimensional SOC matrix in the previous section is not automatically cut into two dimensions here, nor is Q converted into actual atomic displacement.

sections.title: obtains two potential energy surfaces after diagonalization
sections.text: Electronic eigenvalues are ±|g|ρ, where ρ is the radius in the two-dimensional coordinate space. Adding elastic energy gives upper and lower adiabatic surfaces. For g≠0, the origin is a conical intersection; its lower state is not unique, so an arbitrary numerical eigenvector has no unique orbital interpretation.

sections.title: The minimum value comes from the analytical derivative
sections.text: The lower surface’s radial derivative is Kρ−|g|, so its minimum radius is |g|/K and its energy lies g²/(2K) below the origin. The program reports this analytical global minimum even outside the current 2D window, and the radial curve includes that radius. At g=0, the origin is the only minimum.

sections.title: A circular valley is not a continuous rotational symmetry of an actual crystal
sections.text: linear model only relies on ρ, so the minimum set is a circle when g≠0. This is an accidental continuous degeneracy of the model; higher-order couplings and environmental anisotropy can choose discrete directions. The current calculation does not include nuclear kinetic energy, zero-point vibrations, dynamic JT tunneling, temperature, or multiple electron occupancy; it provides a mechanistic example of structural distortion classroom rather than a real material phase diagram.
sections.formula: Radial curvature K>0; round valley tangential curvature is 0 (only this linear adiabatic model)

lessons.title: The phase of one quantum state and the distance between states
lessons.summary: Understand the quantum metric through projectors, first distinguishing wavefunction phases, orbital bases and actual changes of state.

sections.title: Remove the irrelevant overall phase
sections.text: Eigenvectors of one isolated band can be multiplied pointwise by e^(iα(k)) while projector P=|u⟩⟨u| remains unchanged. The ordinary derivative ∂u changes with α and its norm cannot directly define physical distance. The quantum geometric tensor first removes changes parallel to the original state using 1−P, retaining distinguishable changes between state rays.

sections.title: The real part gives the metric; the imaginary part gives curvature
sections.text: We use Berry connection A=i⟨u|∂u⟩, so Q=g−iΩ/2. The metric measures the second-order departure of neighboring-state overlap from 1; curvature measures the geometric phase around a small parameter-space loop. For the lower band of H=d·σ, the projector is set by n=d/|d|. Multiplying all energies by a positive number leaves n unchanged, so the gap can change while geometry in this fixed basis remains unchanged.

sections.title: Build intuition from SSH limits
sections.text: At t₁=0,t₂=1, the SSH lower band winds once around the equator across the Brillouin zone, giving g_{kk}=1/4 in the current periodic orbital basis. At t₂=0, its eigenprojector is k-independent and g_{kk}=0. SSH is one-dimensional: this module reports its 1D metric and Zak phase, not a 2D Chern number. Changing the cell or orbital embedding is not merely a U(1) phase change of a band eigenvector.

lessons.title: From local Berry curvature to Zak and Chern invariants
lessons.summary: Specify the band, coordinate orientation, and sign convention so discrete loops and continuous curvature yield comparable conclusions.

sections.title: Fix the QWZ model and occupied band
sections.text: This module selects the negative-energy lower band, places the chemical potential in the gap at zero, and defines area orientation by kx followed by ky. m=−1 gives C=+1, while m=+1 gives C=−1. Changing the Berry-connection sign, choosing the upper band, or reversing coordinates changes signs; align conventions before comparing software. These numbers belong to a teaching model, not predictions for a real material.
sections.formula: H=s[sin kx σx+sin ky σy+(m+cos kx+cos ky)σz]; Ω_{xy}=n·(∂_x n×∂_y n)/2（lower band)

sections.title: Join neighboring states into a closed loop
sections.text: Removing the modulus of neighboring eigenstate overlaps gives U_μ. Gauge phases appear at each link's endpoints but cancel around a closed loop; closing links across Brillouin-zone boundaries must also be included. In this site's convention, FHS plaquette flux is minus the phase of the loop product. Multiplying links along the one-dimensional SSH Brillouin zone gives the Zak phase, defined only modulo 2π.

sections.title: A topological number does not determine all local geometry
sections.text: At m=3, QWZ has total Chern number 0 but may retain nonzero local curvature and metric; positive and negative contributions cancel in the integral. Pure two-band states satisfy det g=Ω²/4 and tr g≥|Ω|. These constrain local geometry, but a large metric at one point, a local curvature peak or a single heatmap cannot independently determine global topology.

lessons.title: Why an integer is insufficient: gap closure and convergence
lessons.summary: Compare analytic gaps, discrete FHS, curvature integration, and gauge tests to detect failures hidden by coarse meshes.

sections.title: A finite mesh can miss an actual gap closing
sections.text: QWZ closes its gap at m=−2,0,2. An odd mesh starting at −π omits Γ, so its sampled minimum gap can remain positive at m=−2. The program uses the model's global analytic direct gap and does not report lower-band Chern/Zak values if the gap closes or falls below the isolation threshold; geometry at local nondegenerate points can still be displayed.

sections.title: A discrete integer and integral convergence are different checks
sections.text: FHS gives an integer when discrete-link conditions are satisfied, yet a coarse mesh may fail to resolve concentrated curvature. This tool compares meshes N and 2N−1, link overlaps, maximum plaquette flux and the known model topology. Unreliable primary numerical results are left blank. A direct Riemann sum of analytic curvature can converge more slowly, so its error is listed separately.
sections.formula: Gap + nonsingular overlaps + flux diagnostics + mesh comparison; an integer result ≠ convergence

sections.title: Use the phase slider for a reproducible gauge test
sections.text: The slider changes eigenstate phases point by point, altering complex components while preserving projectors, overlap magnitudes and closed-loop topology. This tests gauge handling only, not model completeness or mesh adequacy. Save the Hamiltonian, basis convention, gap diagnostics and convergence table in the research record, rather than a single integer.
sections.formula: u′(k)=e^(iα(k))u(k); P′=P, g′=g, Ω′=Ω, and the closed-loop phase is unchanged

lessons.title: Which electrons are involved transport : Fermi thermal window and velocity
lessons.summary: Understand velocity square weighting on the complete Brillouin zone starting from the difference between fill number and current response.

sections.title: Occupying electrons does not mean conducting electrons
sections.text: fills the integral using the Fermi function f; the linear response is also determined by −∂f/∂E by selecting a thermal window with a width of about kBT near the chemical potential. Deep energy levels, even when almost fully occupied, rarely change the current flow. Observe how the window samples the originally discrete grid energy levels as you change the temperature.

sections.title: The same energy can have speeds in different directions
sections.text: The ratio tᵧ/tₓ controls hopping anisotropy. Density of states is not conductance: transport also weights vᵢvⱼ. Coordinate rotations must transform both velocity components and tensors; multiplying one representative velocity direction by an irreducible star’s size does not recover the full tensor.

sections.title: From dispersion to complete BZ integration
sections.text: High-symmetry band paths can locate degeneracies and crossings but do not supply Brillouin-zone integration weights. This module checks a complete periodic mesh and uniform weights point by point. Teaching data come from an independent tight-binding model, not fits to GaAs, Si or other materials.

lessons.title: Seebeck sign and open-circuit electronic thermal conductivity
lessons.summary: Use energy moments to explain thermoelectric signs on the electron and empty-state sides, distinguishing bare heat-current response from zero-current thermal conductivity.

sections.title: thermoelectric Response measurement thermal window asymmetry
sections.text: adopts the convention of electron charge −e, open circuit E=S∇T. L₁ additionally weights E−μ: Seebeck is determined by how much the upper and lower parts of the window offset each other. The low-filled conduction band side is usually negative, and the high-filled empty side can be positive. However, for real multi-band materials, the sign cannot be judged just by the label.

sections.title: Open-circuit thermal conductivity requires subtracting thermoelectric backflow
sections.text: A temperature gradient drives particle flow; the open-circuit electric field cancels net charge current and changes heat flow. Electronic thermal conductivity therefore subtracts the L₁L₀⁻¹L₁ contribution. The program checks positive semidefiniteness of the covariance and reports significant negative values as numerical problems. Phonon thermal conductivity is absent, so actual material ZT cannot be calculated.

sections.title: Applicable range of constant τ
sections.text: The same scalar and energy-independent τ cancels in the ratio of S, and σ and κₑ are both proportional to τ. Change τ to 10 or 30 fs to verify scaling. Energy-dependent scattering reweights the thermal window and this elimination conclusion does not apply.

lessons.title: 2D units, complete data and grid convergence
lessons.summary: avoids four common misjudgments such as vacuum layer, repeated spin, path integration and low-temperature false peaks.

sections.title: Two-dimensional sheet coefficients must not depend on vacuum thickness
sections.text: Two-dimensional results are normalized by cell area, giving sheet electrical conductance in S and electronic thermal conductance in W/K. Three-dimensional volume-normalized conductivities use S/m and W/(m·K). Conversion to bulk units requires a physical thickness; simulation vacuum is not material thickness.
sections.formula: Ω₂D=A, Ω₃D=V; σ₂D=σ₃D× physical thickness (when clearly defined)

sections.title: input energy band set determines the count meaning
sections.text: Electron filling only counts the imported energy bands; the number of empty states is the unoccupied part of these energy bands, and semiconductor doping is not automatically defined. If the input has two spin channels explicitly listed, the degeneracy should be set to 1. The velocity must be Cartesian m/s, the energy must be eV, and the grid, energy, and velocity must correspond one to one.

sections.title: Compare grids first, then interpret peaks
sections.text: The lower the temperature, the narrower the Fermi derivative. Valid transport When there are too few sampled states, moving μ will sweep through the discrete grid energy levels and produce spurious peaks. The program gives the current μ/T difference between the two grids; this does not prove convergence of the entire scan. When the hot window weight is too small or the matrix is ​​ill-conditioned, S and κ are represented by null and cannot be replaced by 0.
sections.formula: x=(E−μ)/(kBT); Check σ grid difference and µV/K change of S

exercises.title: Deduced from the center of gravity constraint crystal field energy level
exercises.prompt: only considers single electron d orbitals, no SOC and no tetragonal terms, and takes the positive splitting amount Δ=1 eV.

steps.prompt: What two groups are the five d orbitals divided into in Oh?
steps.hint: Count xy, yz, xz and the remaining two orbits.
steps.explanation: t₂g includes xy, yz, xz, e_g includes x²−y² and 3z²−r², and the total dimension is 3+2=5.

steps.prompt: What are the correct conditions for taking the center of gravity of orbital energy to zero?
steps.hint: Weight the energy barycenter by orbital multiplicities.
steps.explanation: triple t₂g and double e_g each contribute 3E_t and 2E_e.

steps.prompt: Using E_e−E_t=1 as well, what are the two energies?
steps.hint: into 3E_t+2(E_t+1)=0.
steps.explanation: E_t=−2/5 eV and E_e=3/5 eV: the separation is 1 and the orbital energy barycenter is zero.

steps.prompt: For ideal Td with a positive splitting of 1 eV, which statement is correct?
choices: low e is −0.6, high t₂ is 0.4, no g is added to the label
low t₂g is −0.4, high e_g is 0.6
Only the number of orbitals can change, not their ordering
steps.hint: The doublet lies lower in Td, which has no inversion.
steps.explanation: 2(−0.6)+3(0.4)=0; e/t₂ tag of Td has no g/u. This parameter comparison is not a quantitative prediction of true coordination transitions.

exercises.title: Analytical SOC limit and Kramers pairs
exercises.prompt: Let crystal field Δ, Ds, and Dt be all 0, and take l=2, s=1/2, and λ=0.2 eV.

steps.prompt: Which two j are allowed for angular momentum coupling?
steps.hint: has a single electron spin of 1/2, j=l±s.
steps.explanation: l=2 is coupled with s=1/2 to obtain j=3/2, 5/2, corresponding to 4 and 6 states.

steps.prompt: For j=3/2, what are the L·S eigenvalue and energy?
steps.hint: Substitute [j(j+1)−6−3/4]/2.
steps.explanation: (15/4−6−3/4)/2=−3/2, multiply by λ to get −0.3 eV; the other six states are +0.2 eV.

steps.prompt: After changing λ to −0.2 eV, which group is lower?
choices: The two groups must still be degenerate
steps.hint: All SOC eigenvalues change sign with λ.
steps.explanation: j=5/2 energy is λ=−0.2 eV; j=3/2 is −3λ/2=+0.3 eV.

steps.prompt: With a crystal field but no magnetic field, which graphical interpretation is most reliable?
choices: The shape of any single degenerate eigenvector is unique
The group-averaged angular density is invariant under a change of basis within the degenerate subspace; the levels retain Kramers pairing.
10 ground states means there are 10 electrons
steps.hint: distinguishes between N-dimensional single electron basis and electron number, and uses T²=−1.
steps.explanation: time reversal Keep Kramers pairwise degenerate, and average after projection to the entire group to avoid mistaking any eigenbase selection for physical differences.

exercises.title: hand calculation of round valley and stabilization energy of E⊗e
exercises.prompt: Take g=1 eV, K=2 eV, Q₂, Q₃ as dimensionless coordinates; here only the adiabatic potential energy surface is obtained.

steps.prompt: What are the two eigenvalues ​​of the electron matrix g(Q₂τx+Q₃τz)?
steps.hint: The square of the matrix is ​​g²(Q₂²+Q₃²)I.
steps.explanation: Define ρ=√(Q₂²+Q₃²), the electron energy is ±|g|ρ, and add the same Kρ²/2.

steps.prompt: What is the minimum radius of the lower potential energy surface V−=ρ²−ρ?
steps.hint: Differentiate with respect to ρ: 2ρ−1=0.
steps.explanation: ρ₀=|g|/K=1/2. The radial second derivative is K=2>0.

steps.prompt: What are the minimum energy and the positive stabilization energy?
steps.hint: Substitute ρ=1/2 into ρ²−ρ.
steps.explanation: V_min=−g²/(2K)=−1/4 eV, the energy is reduced by 1/4 eV relative to the origin.

steps.prompt: What is the most accurate conclusion about equal energy in all directions of the same radius?
choices: A real crystal must have continuous spatial rotation symmetry
You must choose a direction at random, which is called the only ground state.
The linear model has an accidental circular valley; higher-order terms can select discrete directions
steps.hint: Only ρ appears in potential energy, not azimuth .
steps.explanation: The round valley belongs to this truncated model; without nuclear kinetic energy, tunneling or higher-order coupling, it cannot be regarded as equivalent to the full structural and dynamic conclusions of real materials.

exercises.title: From state rays to the SSH quantum metric
exercises.prompt: Consider the SSH limit t₁=0,t₂=1 in a fixed periodic orbital basis. Separate phase, projector and geometry step by step.

steps.prompt: Under u→e^(iα)u, how does P=|u⟩⟨u| change?
steps.hint: The bra and ket phases are complex conjugates.
steps.explanation: The phase cancels in the outer product; the projector records only the state ray.

steps.prompt: Why does Q project ∂u with (1−P)?
steps.hint: The derivative along the original state includes an arbitrary phase change.
steps.explanation: It removes the gauge-dependent component parallel to |u⟩, retaining distinguishable changes of state.

steps.prompt: For n=(cos k,sin k,0), ∂kn has length 1. What is g_{kk}?
steps.hint: The two-band formula has a factor 1/4.

steps.prompt: What happens if the entire Hamiltonian is multiplied by positive 3?
steps.hint: n=d/|d| is unchanged and energies are multiplied by 3.
choices: The gap triples; the metric in the current basis is unchanged
Zak must become 3π without taking modulo
steps.explanation: Quantum geometry follows projectors rather than the energy scale. Arbitrary energy rescaling therefore cannot be interpreted as a state change.

exercises.title: Signs, local geometry and global topology
exercises.prompt: Using A=i⟨u|∂u⟩, the QWZ lower band, and area orientation kx→ky, check the interpretation of Chern numbers step by step.

steps.prompt: In this site's convention, how is curvature related to the imaginary part of Q_{xy}?
steps.hint: Q=g−iΩ/2。
steps.explanation: The convention gives Ω_{xy}=−2 Im Q_{xy}; it must not be mixed with the opposite sign convention for the connection.

steps.prompt: For the same gapped band, what happens to C when the integration-coordinate directions x and y are exchanged?
steps.hint: Oriented area and curvature components both reflect antisymmetry; reversing the integration orientation changes the sign.
choices: It changes sign under reversed orientation
steps.explanation: Actively reversing the chosen orientation reverses the sign of C; specify the coordinate orientation used.

steps.prompt: For QWZ at m=3, does C=0 imply zero metric and curvature at every k?
steps.hint: A zero integral may result from cancellation of locally nonzero contributions.
choices: Only when the mesh size is odd
steps.explanation: A topological total does not contain all local geometric information.

steps.prompt: Which relation does the local geometry of a two-dimensional two-band pure state satisfy?
steps.hint: The quantum geometric tensor receives a contribution from one direction orthogonal to the occupied state.
steps.explanation: Two-band pure states saturate the determinant relation in a two-dimensional parameter space, but do not generally require gxx=gyy.

exercises.title: Inverse question: is an integer on a coarse mesh sufficient?
exercises.prompt: Take QWZ with m=−2, s=1 and a 31×31 mesh starting at −π. Decide which conclusions the program should report.

steps.prompt: What is the analytic direct gap 2min(|m+2|,|m|,|m−2|)?
steps.hint: Substitute m=−2 into the three absolute values.
steps.explanation: The gap closes at Γ, so the global lower band is not isolated.

steps.prompt: If the mesh misses Γ and the sampled minimum gap is positive, can a valid Chern number be reported?
steps.hint: Band isolation must be checked throughout the Brillouin zone, not only at sampled points.
choices: No; the analytic gap closure takes precedence, and the main topological value remains blank
Yes; all sampled points are gapped
steps.explanation: Analytic diagnostics prevent a missed gap closure from being misidentified as a gapped topological phase.

steps.prompt: Another gapped parameter set yields integers on both coarse and fine meshes. Must curvature-integration error still be examined?
steps.hint: The link-variable method and an ordinary Riemann integral are different numerical methods.
choices: No; all integrals are automatically exact
Yes; discrete integer quantization cannot replace convergence of another integral
Check only whether the wavefunction is real
steps.explanation: Especially near a phase transition, concentrated local curvature can make ordinary integration converge slowly.

steps.prompt: What does invariance of the closed-loop value under random or smooth eigenstate rephasing at every k demonstrate?
steps.hint: This checks gauge handling, not complete physical validity.
choices: This proves that a real material is a topological insulator
It proves the mesh is sufficiently dense
It supports U(1) gauge invariance of the implementation; gap and convergence checks are still needed
steps.explanation: Passing a gauge check does not exclude gap closure, undersampling, or limitations of the model's applicability.

exercises.title: Derive conductivity and anisotropy from the Fermi window
exercises.prompt: defines a complete two-dimensional single-band grid, constant τ, and no magnetic field. Stepwise construction of directional conductance.

steps.prompt: Which weight determines the response near the chemical potential at small electric fields?
choices: only looks at the lowest energy state
steps.hint: Distinguishes total occupancy from changes in response to small perturbations.
steps.explanation: linear response uses the Fermi derivative, and the thermal window width changes with kBT.

steps.prompt: What velocity factor enters the x-direction conductivity integral?
steps.hint: Current and distribution corrections each give one velocity.
steps.explanation: σₓₓ/τ=e²(g/Ω)Σw vₓ²(−∂f/∂E)。

steps.prompt: Can a two-dimensional conductivity integral be computed from energies and velocities only along Γ–X–M?
choices: Yes, just give equal weight to each point
No, complete BZ volume sampling is required
Yes, as long as the path is denser
steps.hint: The one-dimensional path does not cover the two-dimensional BZ measure.
steps.explanation: The dense path is still not a complete two-dimensional integral, and the missing areas cannot be filled with points.

steps.prompt: Keeping the dispersion parameter t unchanged and enlarging the two-dimensional lattice constant a twice, how does σ/τ change?
steps.hint: Squared velocity contributes a² and area normalization contributes 1/a².
steps.explanation: v² and area scale by the same factor, leaving sheet conductance/τ unchanged; electron sheet density falls to 1/4.

exercises.title: thermoelectric Sign, open circuit correction and τ scaling
exercises.prompt: takes the electron charge −e, open circuit E=S∇T, and compares the energy moment in the thermal window.

steps.prompt: particle-hole symmetric half-filled, what is L₁?
steps.hint: E−μ is an odd weight, and transport is distributed symmetrically on both sides.
steps.explanation: Positive and negative contributions to L₁ cancel; with invertible L₀, S=0.

steps.prompt: If L₁ is positive and is a single decoupling direction, what is the sign of S?
steps.hint: e>0 while the electron charge is −e.
steps.explanation: S=−L₁/(eTL₀), L₀>0, so negative.

steps.prompt: Which formula should be used for κₑ/τ under zero current condition?
steps.hint: The open circuit electric field cancels the particle flow and changes the heat flow.
steps.explanation: must deduct the thermoelectric reflow term, and the bare L₂/T is not an open circuit electronic thermal conductivity.

steps.prompt: What happens if we increase the same constant τ from 10 fs to 30 fs?
choices: σ, κₑ, S are all multiplied by 3
σ and κₑ are multiplied by 3, S remains unchanged
steps.hint: S is the ratio of the same τ-weighted integral.
steps.explanation: The constant τ cancels in S; this conclusion does not apply to the energy dependence τ.

exercises.title: Diagnosis of low-temperature spurious peaks and input counts
exercises.prompt: A very sharp Seebeck peak appears in your two-dimensional calculation. Step-by-step verification of input and convergence.

steps.prompt: There are two explicit upper and lower spin energy bands. How much should spinDegeneracy be set?
steps.hint: Do not multiply the degrees of freedom already listed.
steps.explanation: Each explicit spin band no longer has double spin degeneracy and should be set to 1.

steps.prompt: How should sheet conductance be normalized for a two-dimensional input cell containing 20 Å of vacuum?
choices: uses physical two-dimensional unit cell area
steps.hint: Sheet coefficients must not depend on arbitrary computational vacuum thickness.
steps.explanation: The 2D module normalizes by area; bulk coefficients additionally require a defined physical thickness.

steps.prompt: What explanation is supported first for the spikes moving or disappearing after mesh densification?
choices: Low temperature thermal window has not converged
steps.hint: compares kBT width with discrete energy level spacing.
steps.explanation: grid artifact peaks cannot be interpreted as material features and need to be refined and verified for the full scan.

steps.prompt: S returns null under extremely low carrier conditions. What should be done?
choices: is changed to 0 and drawn into the curve
Keep undefined results and report ill-conditioning diagnostics
steps.hint: Having no reliable value does not mean that the physical quantity is zero.
steps.explanation: Leave null and check thermal windows, band ranges and grids instead of forging determined values.

cases.title: NiO background: localized octahedrons and multi-electron boundaries
cases.summary: Connect the existing NiO structure and magnetic material cases to the local d orbital grouping to distinguish the single electron crystal field diagram from d⁸ multiplet .
cases.kind: Real material coordination background + single electron teaching model
cases.assumption: The d⁸ multi-electron interaction of Ni²⁺ is not in this 10×10 single electron model; the parameters are original teaching values ​​and do not predict NiO high and low spin, magnetic ground state or measured d–d excitation.

cases.title: Ideal tetrahedral cluster: changing coordination, not changing coordinate convention
cases.summary: Compare the ideal background of four equidistant ligands to six equidistant ligands and observe the e/t₂ ordering and d-orbital angle distribution.
cases.assumption: The real compound is not specified, and the potential energy is not recalculated from the ligand position; Δ, Ds, Dt, and λ are all given parameters, and the ligand bond length remains in the visual unit 1.

cases.title: Jahn–Teller mechanism: electron energy and distortion cost
cases.summary: Use analysis E⊗e Tsuburaya to understand how electron splitting compensates for elastic energy, and connect to existing structural distortion and Landau classes.
cases.assumption: Q₂/Q₃ is a dimensionless reduced coordinate; it is not an automatically generated standard crystal model, nor is it g/K fitted from the real structure. Does not include nuclear kinetic energy, dynamic JT, SOC, or phase transition temperature.

cases.title: Dimerized chain: connect band unfolding, Zak phase, and quantum metric
cases.summary: Starting from the existing alternating-hopping chain, compare two dimerizations and state-space distances with fixed intracell/intercell bond conventions.
cases.kind: SSH teaching model; polyacetylene provides historical context
cases.assumption: Only a spinless two-band chain at fixed parameters is calculated. No self-consistent electron– phonon  structure of actual polyacetylene is solved, and Zak/2π is not treated as convention-independent absolute material polarization.

cases.title: QWZ: different local geometries within one Chern class
cases.summary: Vary the mass parameter and energy scale to observe their distinct effects on heatmaps, topological invariants, and gaps.
cases.assumption: The QWZ parameters are original teaching settings, not a fit to an actual magnetic material. The lower-band Chern number is not a calculation of real conductivity, finite-temperature response, or boundary transport.

cases.title: Missing gap closure: give computational results checkable limits
cases.summary: Use the odd mesh of m=−2 to observe disagreement between a sampled gap and analytic gap closure, and practice saving complete diagnostics.
cases.assumption: This model has a known analytic gap. General materials require a separate reliable global band-isolation check rather than reuse of this formula. This module does not automatically diagnose arbitrary first-principles bands.

cases.title: Two-dimensional anisotropic strips: from tensors to thermoelectric symbols
cases.summary: Use the same finite wide energy band to observe the x/y conductance difference, negative S on the electron side and positive S on the empty side.
cases.assumption: does not fit the specific material; given transitions and constant τ, Berry/Hall and interaction corrections are ignored.

cases.title: Three-dimensional cubic electronic strip: isometric response and counting
cases.summary: Compare three directions, check the isotropicity of σ tensor and the unit of carrier body density.
cases.assumption: is a simple cubic single band, and the teaching transition parameters do not correspond to the multi-valley energy bands of silicon or other actual crystals.

cases.title: From suspicious spike to reproducible transport
cases.summary: Run the low-temperature coarse mesh counterexample first, then add temperature or mesh to check local convergence and electronic thermal conductivity boundaries.
cases.assumption: complete uniform BZ input still requires physical band window and velocity convergence; phonon does not include thermal conductivity and does not output true ZT.
